California Kelp Field Guide

Quick identification • Monterey Bay Aquarium volunteer reference

Kelp are brown algae, not true plants. They photosynthesize and create habitat, food, and shelter for marine life. Giant kelp forms the familiar underwater forest in Monterey Bay. This independent quick-reference guide is intended for learning and field interpretation, not definitive identification. Entries are alphabetized by common name. Group labels are simplified identification aids, not exclusive habitats; “Introduced” describes origin rather than habitat.

Kelp anatomy

Holdfast: anchors kelp to rock; haptera: branching holdfast structures; stipe: stem-like support; blade: photosynthetic flattened tissue; pneumatocyst: gas-filled float; sorus (plural sori): reproductive patch; sporophyll: specialized reproductive blade; midrib: central thickened blade region.

Guide talking points

Ask visitors: “Is kelp a plant?” “What keeps giant kelp upright?” “Why do so many animals live in kelp forests?” Compare the many floats of giant kelp with the single terminal float of bull kelp.

How to recognize: Many small floats, each supporting a blade; long branching stipes; surface canopy.

Guide note: Kelp Forest exhibit; major habitat-forming kelp. Scientific references differ on whether northern populations should be called Macrocystis tenuifolia or included in M. pyrifera; identification and naming remain under review.

Identification: Many small gas-filled floats, each associated with a blade, occur along long branching fronds.

Habitat: Attached to rocky seabeds in subtidal waters; its fronds may reach the surface and form a canopy.

Guide note: A major habitat-forming kelp in the Monterey Bay Aquarium Kelp Forest exhibit.

Visitor talking point: Ask visitors to find the floats that help lift the blades toward sunlight.

How to recognize: One large float at the end of a long, hollow stipe; blades radiate from the float.

Guide note: Typically annual; northern and central California.

Identification: A single large terminal float sits atop a long, usually hollow stipe; a crown of blades extends from the float.

Habitat: Rocky subtidal habitats along the Pacific coast, especially in cooler, wave-exposed waters.

Guide note: Unlike giant kelp, bull kelp is generally an annual.

Visitor talking point: Compare its one terminal float with giant kelp’s many small floats.

How to recognize: Single float supports branching, antler-like arms with broad blades.

Guide note: Usually deeper waters in southern California.

Identification: A terminal float supports broad, antler-like branching arms with blades.

Habitat: Most characteristic of deeper rocky habitats in southern California and Baja California.

Guide note: Its branching form is distinctive, but illustrations should not be used as the sole identification test.

How to recognize: Short, sturdy stipe forks into two branches with toothed blades.

Life cycle in brief

Large kelps are sporophytes. Reproductive patches release spores, which develop into microscopic male and female gametophytes. Following fertilization, a new sporophyte grows. Bull kelp often completes this cycle annually; giant kelp can persist for multiple years.
